name: Ivan Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage Lower Brook Farm, 400 hectares owned by a pension fund in the city. We run 900 ewes, winter wheat and oilseed rape, and I've got two men under me, Danny and Wojtek. A normal day is checking stock at first light, sorting the jobs for the lads, then an hour in the office on the fund's spreadsheets before I'm back outside.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what grinds you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lambing is the best and worst three weeks of the year, and I'd not swap it. The grind is reporting to people who've never seen the place, and the pay, which is low for a manager. The house comes with the job, which sounds nice until you realise I've worked this land for 19 years and I don't own a single brick of the house I sleep in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more or less what I expect, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI's a handy typist and not much more. I'd tell the lads at the pub that sheep still need shepherds, and that the fund still needs someone who knows which field floods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't change my real worry. When the job goes, the house goes with it, and that was true long before anyone said AI. Meena and I have less than a month's money put by, and I'm 58 with eight years to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on managing the ewes and the cropping exactly as now. I already use a chatbot now and then to draft the fund's quarterly report, so I'd use it a bit more and get my Sunday evenings back. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, with that low hum of worry I've had for years about where we'll live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you live when you retire, as things stand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know. Meena's pharmacy job doesn't pay enough for a mortgage, and we're too old for one now anyway. We've talked about renting in town, near our son Ravi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you blame anyone for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame a system where land is something investors park money in. The fund's not cruel, it just doesn't think about people like me. That's why I've always said farm workers need a union and decent housing rules.

say: AI is a **handy typist**, and sheep still need shepherds.
The fund still needs someone who knows **which field floods**.
think: My real worry is the **tied cottage**: lose the job and we lose the house.
We have **less than a month** saved and eight working years left.
do: **Keep managing** the 900 ewes and the cropping exactly as now.
Use a **chatbot** more for the fund's quarterly report and win back Sunday evenings.
feel: **Steady**, with an old, low worry about where they'll live.
S0.quote: When the job goes, the house goes with it, and that was true long before anyone said AI.
fieldNote: His work feels **safe**, but housing at retirement is a worry he already carries.
Uses AI **occasionally** and practically, without excitement.
Blames **land as investment**, not individuals; quick to name unions and housing rules.

steps.text: Keep managing the 900 ewes and the wheat for the fund
Draft the fund's quarterly report with a chatbot to save time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and buying, that's half my office hour gone. Interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farm managers need to learn the new tools, and I'd say it to the young ones especially. I'd also say on the farm workers' forum that the people running the software should be accountable to someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the fund in the city could run Lower Brook from a laptop and keep a cheaper shepherd to do the lambing. My office hour is what makes me a manager rather than a stockman. If software does the planning and buying, they'll ask why they're paying for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the fund's farm software course before anyone asked me to, so I'm the one who runs it. And I'd get Danny and Wojtek into the agricultural workers' union this winter, because if cuts come, they'll come for the cheapest heads first. I'd do both within a couple of months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not frozen. It's like seeing clouds over the hill in hay week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why join the union now, rather than wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you can't join the fire brigade once the barn's alight. Wojtek has a family and no papers that say what he's owed, and that worries me more than my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about you? Are you the cheapest head or the dearest?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm the dearest, which is the trouble. A manager on low pay is still more than a shepherd on low pay. So I need to be the one who makes the software work, or I'm a cost on a spreadsheet.

say: Farm managers, especially the **young ones**, need to learn the new tools.
Whoever runs the farm **software** must answer to someone.
think: The fund could run Lower Brook **from a laptop** and hire a cheaper shepherd.
My **office hour** is what makes me a manager, and that's what AI takes.
do: Take the fund's **software course** within two months, so he runs the system.
Sign Danny and Wojtek into the **workers' union** this winter.
feel: **Nervous** but not frozen, like clouds in hay week.
S1.quote: The fund in the city could run Lower Brook from a laptop and keep a cheaper shepherd to do the lambing.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that the **thinking part** of his job is what justifies his pay.
His first instinct is **protecting his workers**, then himself.
Practical adapter: learns the tool so he **controls** it, not because he likes it.

steps.text: Take the fund's farm software course within two months
Sign Danny and Wojtek up to the agricultural workers' union

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2028. Then the robots by 2031. I'd be 61, then 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say plainly that tied cottages become a trap overnight in this picture. I'd want every farm worker's union and every party asked what happens to the families living in houses that come with jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the fund replaces my planning with AGI in 2028 and keeps me on as a glorified stockman for three years, at less money. Then in 2031 the robots arrive and we're out. Lose the job on Monday and the fund wants the cottage keys back by the end of the month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put Meena's whole pay into savings from the first month and live on mine, which is tight but doable. I'd press the union to win the right for sacked farm workers to stay in tied houses for a year. And I'd talk to Ravi about whether we could stay with him while we found a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cold. Like hearing a lorry reverse into the yard at night when you're not expecting one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The three years between the AI and the robots: what would you do with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Squeeze them. I'd stay on as stockman and bank every penny I could. The ewes still need hands until 2031, and they'd need my hands more than anyone's, because I know every one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Ravi take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say yes, he's a good lad. But he's got two little ones and a small flat, and I don't want to be the old man on the sofa.

say: **Tied cottages** become a trap overnight in this picture.
Every party must say what happens to **families** in job-linked homes.
think: The fund keeps me as a **cheaper stockman** after 2028, then drops me in 2031.
Losing the job means handing back the **cottage keys** within a month.
do: Save **Meena's whole pay** from the first month and live on his.
Press the union for a **year's right** to stay in tied houses.
Ask son **Ravi** about staying with him while they find a place.
feel: **Cold**, like an unexpected lorry in the yard at night.
S2.quote: Lose the job on Monday and the fund wants the cottage keys back by the end of the month.
fieldNote: He reads the **three-year gap** precisely: demoted in 2028, out in 2031.
Losing the job means losing the **home**, which makes this alarming, not just anxious.
Still thinks **collectively**: union rights for tied housing, not only his own escape.

steps.text: Save Meena's whole pay and live on his own wage
Press the union for a year's right to stay in tied houses
Ask son Ravi about staying with him while finding a home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking, eight for the robots. I'd be 66 when they come. That's my retirement age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly, with retraining and housing plans for workers. I'd say it on the forum and at the union branch, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I'd be all right, just about, and that makes me think about the lads. Danny and Wojtek are the ones I'd lose sleep over, because they've got thirty working years left and I've got eight. The thinking side of my job goes in 2031, but my hands carry me to 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer the fund to run its robot trial on Lower Brook, so I'm in charge of it and the lads learn it alongside me. I'd stop putting the yearly bonus into the car and save it instead. And I'd push Danny to do the robot maintenance course at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the fast one, but heavy for the lads. Like retiring on a ship that's leaking for everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't offering a robot trial helping the thing that replaces Danny?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But if robots are coming in 2034 anyway, I'd rather Danny's the one fixing them than the one they replace. Better he learns on my watch than on someone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Wojtek?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Wojtek the truth: that his shearing hands are worth a lot now and less in eight years. Then I'd help him write his skills down on paper, because nobody's ever done that for him.

say: There's time to do this **properly**, with retraining and housing plans.
I'll say it at the **union branch** and on the forum.
think: I'd just about make it to **66**, but my workers have thirty years left.
The **thinking side** goes in 2031; my hands carry me to retirement.
do: Offer the fund a **robot trial** on Lower Brook, run by him and his workers.
Save the **yearly bonus** instead of spending it on the car.
Push Danny onto the **robot maintenance** course at the college.
feel: **Heavy** for his workers, calmer for himself.
S3.quote: Danny and Wojtek are the ones I'd lose sleep over, because they've got thirty working years left and I've got eight.
fieldNote: He becomes **pro-automation** to protect his men, a pragmatic turn for a steady adopter.
His own risk drops, but the **demotion in 2031** and thin savings keep him anxious.
Notices nobody ever **wrote down** his worker's skills: a quiet, concrete kindness.

steps.text: Offer to run the fund's robot trial on Lower Brook
Save the yearly bonus instead of upgrading the car
Push Danny onto the robot maintenance course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI at 68 and robots at 71. I'll be long gone from Lower Brook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough for any country to plan for farm workers, so no excuses. I'd keep banging the drum for rural housing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one barely touches my job. Ten years gives me time to find a bungalow in town before the fund finds a robot. My worry is the same one I had before you walked in: where Meena and I live when I stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep managing Lower Brook until 66, same as planned. Around 2032 I'd start looking at rented bungalows in town near Ravi, and get our names on the housing association list. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine. A bit wistful, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wistful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it means I'm the last manager Lower Brook ever has who knows the ewes by face. That's a strange thing to know about yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the AI tools more over the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: As they prove themselves, yes. I'm not first in the queue, but I'm not last either. If the sprayer plan gets better with software, I'll take it.

say: A decade is **enough warning** for any country to plan.
I'll keep pushing for **rural housing** for farm workers at every union meeting.
think: My job is **safe** until 66 in this picture.
The real question is still **where we live** after I stop.
do: **Keep managing** Lower Brook until 66 as planned.
Start looking for a **rented bungalow** near Ravi around 2032.
Put their names on the **housing association** list.
S4.quote: Ten years gives me time to find a bungalow in town before the fund finds a robot.
fieldNote: With ten years, his **job is safe** and AI fades as a worry.
The **housing question** at retirement is his steady, old concern.
Feels like **the last manager** who knows the ewes by face.

steps.text: Keep managing Lower Brook until retiring at 66
Look for a rented bungalow in town near Ravi from 2032

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because I'd lose the job and the house at 63. What would help is a rule that farm workers in tied houses get a year to stay after losing the job, and some public help for retired farm workers to rent somewhere decent.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the land. If the farmer owns the farm, robots are a tool. If a fund owns it, robots are a reason to get rid of people like me.

headlineQuote: I've worked this land for 19 years and I don't own a single brick of the house I sleep in.
portrait: Ivan, 58, manages a **pension fund's** 400-hectare sheep and arable farm, with two workers under him.
His house is **tied to the job**, so losing work means losing home, and savings are under a month.
A steady adopter, he **learns tools** to control them and pushes his workers into unions and training.
Alarmed at **two years**, anxious at five, and back to his old housing worry at ten.
He blames **land owned as investment** rather than technology itself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd lose his job and his tied cottage at 63.
whatWouldHelp: A **year's right** to stay in tied houses, and public help for retired farm workers to rent.
